## Bayesian Posterior of Mentalizing Models

Exp1

```{r}
# In experiment 1, participants know the full distributions of the two jars.
#
# Latent world state d: color of the sampled ball
# Target category c:    identity of the sampled jar
# Agent knowledge k1/2:  distribution of one ball color
# Agent judgment s1/s2:   Jar 1 or Jar 2
#
# The reasoner computes: P(c | s1, s2) = sum_d P(c | d) P(d | s1, s2)
# with
# P(d | s1, s2) ~ P(s1 | d, k1) P(s2 | d, k2) P(d).

#agent response likelihood P(s1 | d, k1), P(s2 | d, k2)
agent_jar_likelihood <- function(
    jar1, jar2,
    color,
    known_color,
    response,
    total_balls,
    tau) {

  # If the observed color is within the agent's knowledge,
  # use its known distribution across the two jars.
  if (color == known_color) {

    p_jar1 <- jar1[[color]] /
      (jar1[[color]] + jar2[[color]])

  } else {

    # For colors outside the agent's knowledge, the remaining
    # probability mass is distributed equally across the two
    # unknown colors.
    unknown_jar1 <- (total_balls - jar1[[known_color]]) / 2
    unknown_jar2 <- (total_balls - jar2[[known_color]]) / 2

    p_jar1 <- unknown_jar1 /
      (unknown_jar1 + unknown_jar2)
  }

  # Convert the agent's posterior beliefs into response probabilities.
  response_prob <- softmax(
    c(p_jar1, 1 - p_jar1),
    tau
  )

  # Responses are represented either as 1/2 or Type1/Type2.
  response_index <- if (is.character(response)) {
    match(response, c("Type1", "Type2"))
  } else {
    as.integer(response)
  }

  response_prob[response_index]
}

# posterior
posterior_exp1 <- function(
    jar1, jar2,
    s1, s2,
    k1, k2,
    tau) {

  total_balls <- 20
  colors <- c("blue", "yellow", "red")

  names(jar1) <- colors
  names(jar2) <- colors

  # Hypothesis space:
  # 3 possible colors x 2 possible source jars = 6 hypotheses.
  hypotheses <- expand.grid(
    color = colors,
    chosen_jar = 1:2,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  weights <- numeric(nrow(hypotheses))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(hypotheses))) {

    color <- hypotheses$color[i]
    chosen_jar <- hypotheses$chosen_jar[i]

    # Prior probability of observing this ball color:
    # P(d)
    total_color <- jar1[[color]] + jar2[[color]]
    p_color <- total_color / (2 * total_balls)

    # Probability of the source jar conditional on color:
    # P(c | d)
    p_jar <- c(
      jar1[[color]],
      jar2[[color]]
    ) / total_color

    # Agent likelihoods:
    # P(s1 | d, k1)
    # P(s2 | d, k2) 
    ll_s1 <- agent_jar_likelihood(
      jar1, jar2,
      color = color,
      known_color = k1,
      response = s1,
      total_balls = total_balls,
      tau = tau
    )

    ll_s2 <- agent_jar_likelihood(
      jar1, jar2,
      color = color,
      known_color = k2,
      response = s2,
      total_balls = total_balls,
      tau = tau
    )


    # P(c, d, s1, s2)
    #  ~  P(c | d)
    #     P(s1 | c, k1)
    #     P(s2 | c, k2)
    #     P(d)
    
    weights[i] <-
      p_jar[chosen_jar] *
      ll_s1 *
      ll_s2 *
      p_color
  }

  # Marginalize over possible ball colors.
  jar_weights <- tapply(
    weights,
    hypotheses$chosen_jar,
    sum
  )

  posterior <- jar_weights / sum(jar_weights)

  # Return P(Jar 2 | s1, s2)
  unname(posterior["2"])
}

 # Define a softmax transformation for expert responses. 
  softmax <- function(x, rtau) {
    exps <- exp(log(x) * rtau)
    probabilities <- exps / sum(exps)
    return(probabilities)
  }
  

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 1 trial predictions
# ------------------------------------------------------------

w_list1 <- function(tau) {

  jar1_list <- list(
    c(4, 15, 1),
    c(1, 6, 13),
    c(1, 4, 15),
    c(1, 4, 15)
  )

  jar2_list <- list(
    c(15, 1, 4),
    c(4, 15, 1),
    c(4, 1, 15),
    c(4, 15, 1)
  )

  # Different-knowledge condition:
  # Agent 1 knows blue; Agent 2 knows yellow.
  response_div <- list(
    c(1, 2),
    c(1, 1),
    c(2, 2),
    c(2, 1)
  )

  # Same-knowledge condition:
  # Both agents know blue.
  response_nodiv <- list(
    c(1, 1),
    c(1, 1),
    c(2, 2),
    c(2, 2)
  )

  posterior <- numeric(8)

  for (i in 1:4) {

    jar1 <- jar1_list[[i]]
    jar2 <- jar2_list[[i]]

    # Different knowledge
    posterior[2 * i - 1] <- posterior_exp1(
      jar1, jar2,
      s1 = response_div[[i]][1],
      s2 = response_div[[i]][2],
      k1 = "blue",
      k2 = "yellow",
      tau = tau
    )

    # Same knowledge
    posterior[2 * i] <- posterior_exp1(
      jar1, jar2,
      s1 = response_nodiv[[i]][1],
      s2 = response_nodiv[[i]][2],
      k1 = "blue",
      k2 = "blue",
      tau = tau
    )
  }

  posterior
}


w_list1(1000)
```

exp2

```{r}
# In Experiment 2, participants have only partial knowledge: they know the number of red balls in each jar but do not know the complete color distributions.
# Therefore, participants do not have direct access to the exact private knowledge k_i held by each social agent. Instead, they consider a finite set of candidate knowledge states k^(m) that are consistent with their own partial knowledge kp.

# The posterior should be computed as:
# P(c | s1, s2, k^p) = sum_d sum_m P(c | d, k^(m), k^p) P(d, k^(m) | s1, s2, k^p) Here k^(m) = (k1^(m),k2^(m))
# with
# P(d, k^(m)| s1, s2, k^p) ~ P(s1, s2 | d, k^(m)) P(d, k^(m) | k^p)
# P(s1, s2 | d, k^(m)) = P(s1| d, k1^(m)) * P(s2| d, k2^(m)) * P(k1^(m)|k^(m)) * P(k2^(m)|k^(m)) 
#                      = P(s1| d, k1^(m)) * P(s2| d, k2^(m))

# P(d, k^(m) | k^p) = P(k^(m) | k^p ) * P(d|k^(m), k^p)
#   d          = latent world state (drawn ball color)
#   c          = target category (jar identity)
#   s_i        = judgment of agent i
#   k^p        = participant's partial knowledge
#   k_i^(m)    = candidate private knowledge state of agent i


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 2 mentalizing posterior
# ------------------------------------------------------------

posterior_mentalizing <- function(
    jar1, jar2,
    s1, s2,
    k1, k2,
    tau) {

  total_balls <- 10
  colors <- c("blue", "yellow", "red")

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Participant's partial knowledge k^p
  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  #
  # Participants directly observe only the number of red balls.
  # Therefore, the numbers of blue and yellow balls remain
  # uncertain.
  #
  # We enumerate all complete jar distributions consistent with
  # k^p, assuming that each jar contains at least one blue and
  # one yellow ball.

  red1 <- jar1[["red"]]
  red2 <- jar2[["red"]]

  jar1_blue_range <- seq(
    1,
    total_balls - red1 - 1
  )

  jar2_blue_range <- seq(
    1,
    total_balls - red2 - 1
  )

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Hypothesis space
  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  #
  # Each hypothesis specifies:
  #
  #   1. a candidate complete distribution consistent with k^p;
  #   2. a candidate latent world state d (ball color);
  #   3. a candidate category c (jar identity).
  #
  # Each candidate complete distribution induces corresponding
  # candidate private knowledge states k_1^(m) and k_2^(m).

  hypotheses <- expand.grid(
    jar1_blue = jar1_blue_range,
    jar2_blue = jar2_blue_range,
    color = colors,
    chosen_jar = 1:2,
    KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ) |>

    mutate(

      # Reconstruct each possible complete distribution of Jar 1
      # consistent with participant knowledge k^p.
      jar1_h = Map(
        function(blue) {
          c(
            blue = blue,
            yellow = total_balls - red1 - blue,
            red = red1
          )
        },
        jar1_blue
      ),

      # Reconstruct each possible complete distribution of Jar 2.
      jar2_h = Map(
        function(blue) {
          c(
            blue = blue,
            yellow = total_balls - red2 - blue,
            red = red2
          )
        },
        jar2_blue
      ),

      # For each candidate knowledge configuration k^(m),
      # calculate the probability of drawing a ball of color d: P(d | k^(m), k^p)
      prior_d = pmap_dbl(
        list(jar1_h, jar2_h, color),
        function(j1, j2, d) {

          (j1[[d]] + j2[[d]]) /
            (2 * total_balls)
        }
      ),

      # Conditional on the candidate world state d and candidate
      # complete distribution k^(m), calculate the probability
      # that the ball originated from each jar. P(c | d, k^(m), k^p)
      #
      # Here, c corresponds to the identity of the sampled jar.

      p_category = pmap_dbl(
        list(chosen_jar, jar1_h, jar2_h, color),
        function(c, j1, j2, d) {

          count1 <- j1[[d]]
          count2 <- j2[[d]]

          p_jar <- c(count1, count2) /
            (count1 + count2)

          p_jar[c]
        }
      )
    ) |>
    rowwise() |>
    # Agent response likelihoods P(s1 | d, k_1^(m)), P(s2 | d, k_2^(m))
    mutate(
      # P(s1 | d, k_1^(m))
      ll_s1 = agent_jar_likelihood(
        jar1 = jar1_h,
        jar2 = jar2_h,
        color = color,
        known_color = k1,
        response = s1,
        total_balls = total_balls,
        tau = tau
      ),
    
      # P(s2 | d, k_2^(m))
      ll_s2 = agent_jar_likelihood(
        jar1 = jar1_h,
        jar2 = jar2_h,
        color = color,
        known_color = k2,
        response = s2,
        total_balls = total_balls,
        tau = tau
      ),
    
     
      # w(c, d, k^(m), s1, s2)
      #   ~ P(c | d, k^(m), k^p)
      #     P(s1 | d, k_1^(m))
      #     P(s2 | d, k_2^(m))
      #     P(d | k^(m), k^p)
      weight = p_category * ll_s1 * ll_s2 * prior_d
    ) |>
    ungroup()


  # Marginalization

  final <- hypotheses |>
    group_by(chosen_jar) |>
    summarise(
      weight = sum(weight),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      posterior = weight / sum(weight)
    )


  # Return the posterior probability that Jar 2 was sampled.
  final |>
    filter(chosen_jar == 2) |>
    pull(posterior)
}



w_list2 <- function(tau) {

  # True jar distributions used to construct the experimental
  # stimuli. Participants themselves observe only the red-ball
  # counts when performing the task.

  jar1_list <- list(
    c(blue = 2, yellow = 7, red = 1),
    c(blue = 1, yellow = 1, red = 8),
    c(blue = 1, yellow = 3, red = 6),
    c(blue = 5, yellow = 4, red = 1)
  )

  jar2_list <- list(
    c(blue = 1, yellow = 1, red = 8),
    c(blue = 1, yellow = 7, red = 2),
    c(blue = 2, yellow = 1, red = 7),
    c(blue = 1, yellow = 2, red = 7)
  )

  # Judgments in the different-knowledge condition:
  # one agent has access to blue-ball information and the other
  # has access to yellow-ball information.
  response_div <- list(
    c("Type2", "Type2"),
    c("Type2", "Type1"),
    c("Type2", "Type2"),
    c("Type1", "Type2")
  )


  # Judgments in the same-knowledge condition:
  # both agents have access to the same color distribution.
  response_nodiv <- list(
    c("Type2", "Type2"),
    c("Type1", "Type1"),
    c("Type2", "Type2"),
    c("Type1", "Type1")
  )


  # Knowledge domain shared by the two agents in each
  # no-diversity trial pair.
  same_knowledge <- c(
    "blue",
    "yellow",
    "blue",
    "blue"
  )


  posterior <- numeric(8)
  for (i in 1:4) {

    jar1 <- jar1_list[[i]]
    jar2 <- jar2_list[[i]]


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Same-knowledge condition
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    posterior[2 * i - 1] <- posterior_mentalizing(
      jar1 = jar1,
      jar2 = jar2,
      s1 = response_nodiv[[i]][1],
      s2 = response_nodiv[[i]][2],
      k1 = same_knowledge[i],
      k2 = same_knowledge[i],
      tau = tau
    )


    # Different-knowledge condition
    posterior[2 * i] <- posterior_mentalizing(
      jar1 = jar1,
      jar2 = jar2,
      s1 = response_div[[i]][1],
      s2 = response_div[[i]][2],
      k1 = "blue",
      k2 = "yellow",
      tau = tau
    )
  }
  posterior
}


# Model predictions
w_list2(1000)
```

```{r}
# ============================================================
# Experiment 3
# ============================================================
#
# Latent world state d:
#   joint ear-foot feature configuration
#
# Target category c:
#   alien Type 1 or Type 2
#
# Agent knowledge k_i:
#   ear expertise or foot expertise
#
# Agent judgment s_i:
#   Type 1 or Type 2
#
# The mentalizing model computes:
#
# P(c | s1, s2)
#   ∝ sum_d
#       P(s1 | d, k1)
#       P(s2 | d, k2)
#       P(d | c)
#       P(c)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Construct participant and expert knowledge
# ------------------------------------------------------------

make_alien_knowledge <- function(a1, b2, total = 10) {

  # Full joint feature distribution available to participants.
  #
  # Rows correspond to:
  #   ear = 0, foot = 0
  #   ear = 1, foot = 0
  #   ear = 0, foot = 1
  #   ear = 1, foot = 1

  full <- expand.grid(
    ear = c(0, 1),
    foot = c(0, 1)
  )

  full$Type1 <- c(
    a1,
    0,
    0,
    total - a1
  )

  full$Type2 <- c(
    0,
    b2,
    total - b2,
    0
  )

  # Ear experts marginalize over foot size.
  ear <- data.frame(
    feature = c(0, 1),
    Type1 = c(
      a1,
      total - a1
    ),
    Type2 = c(
      total - b2,
      b2
    )
  )

  # Foot experts marginalize over ear size.
  foot <- data.frame(
    feature = c(0, 1),
    Type1 = c(
      a1,
      total - a1
    ),
    Type2 = c(
      b2,
      total - b2
    )
  )

  list(
    full = full,
    ear = ear,
    foot = foot
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Expert response likelihood
# ------------------------------------------------------------

expert_likelihood <- function(
    response,
    feature_value,
    expert_type,
    knowledge,
    tau) {

  expert_knowledge <- knowledge[[expert_type]]

  idx <- expert_knowledge$feature == feature_value

  count_type1 <- expert_knowledge$Type1[idx]
  count_type2 <- expert_knowledge$Type2[idx]

  p_type1 <- count_type1 /
    (count_type1 + count_type2)

  response_prob <- softmax(
    c(p_type1, 1 - p_type1),
    tau
  )

  response_index <- match(
    response,
    c("Type1", "Type2")
  )

  response_prob[response_index]
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 3 mentalizing posterior
# ------------------------------------------------------------

posterior_exp3 <- function(
    a1, b2,
    s1, s2,
    expert1, expert2,
    tau) {

  total <- 10
  knowledge <- make_alien_knowledge(a1, b2, total)

  # Hypothesis space:
  # 2 ear states x 2 foot states x 2 alien types = 8 hypotheses.
  hypotheses <- expand.grid(
    ear = c(0, 1),
    foot = c(0, 1),
    type = c("Type1", "Type2"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  weights <- numeric(nrow(hypotheses))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(hypotheses))) {

    ear_state <- hypotheses$ear[i]
    foot_state <- hypotheses$foot[i]
    alien_type <- hypotheses$type[i]

    idx <-
      knowledge$full$ear == ear_state &
      knowledge$full$foot == foot_state

    # Prior over the joint feature state and alien type:
    #
    # P(d, c) = P(d | c) P(c)
    #
    # Both alien types are equally likely a priori.
    p_state_given_type <-
      knowledge$full[[alien_type]][idx] / total

    p_type <- 0.5

    prior <- p_state_given_type * p_type

    # Select the feature visible to each expert.
    feature1 <- if (expert1 == "ear") {
      ear_state
    } else {
      foot_state
    }

    feature2 <- if (expert2 == "ear") {
      ear_state
    } else {
      foot_state
    }

    # P(s1 | d, k1)
    ll_s1 <- expert_likelihood(
      response = s1,
      feature_value = feature1,
      expert_type = expert1,
      knowledge = knowledge,
      tau = tau
    )

    # P(s2 | d, k2)
    ll_s2 <- expert_likelihood(
      response = s2,
      feature_value = feature2,
      expert_type = expert2,
      knowledge = knowledge,
      tau = tau
    )

    # Conditional independence:
    #
    # P(s1, s2 | d, k1, k2)
    #   = P(s1 | d, k1) P(s2 | d, k2)
    weights[i] <- prior * ll_s1 * ll_s2
  }

  # Marginalize over joint ear-foot states.
  type_weights <- tapply(
    weights,
    hypotheses$type,
    sum
  )

  posterior <- type_weights / sum(type_weights)

  # Return P(Type 2 | s1, s2)
  unname(posterior["Type2"])
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 3 trial predictions
# ------------------------------------------------------------

w_list3 <- function(tau) {

  response1 <- c(
    "Type1", "Type2", "Type2", "Type1",
    "Type1", "Type2", "Type1", "Type2",
    "Type1", "Type2", "Type2", "Type1",
    "Type1", "Type2", "Type1", "Type2"
  )

  response2 <- c(
    "Type1", "Type2", "Type1", "Type2",
    "Type1", "Type2", "Type1", "Type2",
    "Type1", "Type2", "Type1", "Type2",
    "Type1", "Type2", "Type1", "Type2"
  )

  a1 <- 2
  b2 <- 3

  posterior <- numeric(16)

  for (i in 1:16) {

    if (i %in% 1:4) {

      # One ear expert and one foot expert.
      # Preserve the original response ordering for Trials 1-4.
      posterior[i] <- posterior_exp3(
        a1, b2,
        s1 = response2[i],
        s2 = response1[i],
        expert1 = "ear",
        expert2 = "foot",
        tau = tau
      )

    } else if (i %in% c(5, 6, 13, 14)) {

      # Two ear experts.
      posterior[i] <- posterior_exp3(
        a1, b2,
        s1 = response1[i],
        s2 = response2[i],
        expert1 = "ear",
        expert2 = "ear",
        tau = tau
      )

    } else if (i %in% c(7, 8, 15, 16)) {

      # Two foot experts.
      posterior[i] <- posterior_exp3(
        a1, b2,
        s1 = response1[i],
        s2 = response2[i],
        expert1 = "foot",
        expert2 = "foot",
        tau = tau
      )

    } else {

      # One ear expert and one foot expert.
      posterior[i] <- posterior_exp3(
        a1, b2,
        s1 = response1[i],
        s2 = response2[i],
        expert1 = "ear",
        expert2 = "foot",
        tau = tau
      )
    }
  }

  posterior
}


w_list3(1000)
```
